title: A lonely galactic island
caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy DDO 190, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Older reddish stars fill the outskirts of this small galaxy, while younger bluish stars shine in its more crowded middle. Pockets of gas heated by stars appear here and there, the most obvious one glowing toward the bottom. Behind it, many distant spiral, elliptical and shapeless galaxies glow. This is DDO 190, a dwarf irregular galaxy, small and without clear structure.

Our Solar System sits in a big spiral with plenty of dwarf companions. DDO 190 has no such company. It lies around nine million light-years away, according to the caption, loosely part of the Messier 94 group, yet its closest dwarf neighbour, DDO 187, is thought to lie at least three million light-years off.
By comparison, the Magellanic Clouds orbit the Milky Way at around a fifth of that distance, and even the Andromeda Galaxy is closer to us than DDO 190 is to its nearest neighbour.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in visible and near-infrared light. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the galaxy's individual stars could never be separated by eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Sidney van der Bergh first recorded DDO 190 in 1959 in the DDO catalogue of dwarf galaxies, named for the David Dunlap Observatory. A version of this image was entered into Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition by Claude Cornen.
alt: A small, shapeless galaxy with reddish stars on its outskirts, bluish stars in its centre, and many distant galaxies behind it.
